titulo_es: The subjunctive in fixed phrases (be that as it may, come what may, so be it)
descripcion_es: Remnants of the subjunctive in formal set expressions: be that as it may, come what may, so be it, suffice it to say, God save…
resumen: Some fixed expressions keep the old English subjunctive (the base form of the verb, often with inversion). They cannot be formed freely: they are learnt as blocks and give a formal, solemn or rhetorical tone.

filas: be that as it may
however that may be, even so (es: sea como sea, aun así)
Be that as it may, the decision is final.
come what may
whatever happens (es: pase lo que pase)
Come what may, we'll finish on time.
so be it
let it be so; I accept it (es: así sea, que así sea)
If they want a fight, so be it.
suffice it to say (that)
it is enough to say that (es: baste decir que)
Suffice it to say that he was not pleased.
far be it from me to + inf.
I have no wish to… (es: lejos de mí la intención de)
Far be it from me to criticise, but…
heaven forbid / God forbid
I hope this never happens (es: Dios no lo quiera)
Heaven forbid that it should happen again.
long live…
may… live / last for a long time (es: viva…)
Long live the king!
God save…
may God protect… (es: Dios salve a…)
God save the Queen.
perish the thought
that idea is unthinkable (es: ni pensarlo, ni lo mencione)
Retire? Perish the thought!
as it were
so to speak (es: por así decirlo)
She is, as it were, the soul of the company.
if need be
if it is necessary (es: si fuera necesario)
We can work at weekends if need be.
be it… or… / be they… or…
whether it is… or… / whether they are… or… (es: ya sea… o…)
Every citizen, be they rich or poor, must pay.
the powers that be
the people in authority (es: las autoridades, los que mandan)
The powers that be have rejected our proposal.
if I were you
in your position, I would… (es: yo que tú)
If I were you, I'd apologise.

items: They are frozen expressions: you do not change the person or the tense (not “be that as it might”, not “came what may”).
Their effect is rhetorical: useful in a presentation to qualify or conclude (Be that as it may…, Suffice it to say…), but do not overuse them.
Far be it from me usually introduces precisely what the speaker claims not to want to do: Far be it from me to interfere, but…

ejemplos.frase: The data are incomplete. Be that as it may, the trend is clear.
ejemplos.traduccion: Los datos están incompletos. Aun así, la tendencia es clara.

ejemplos.frase: Come what may, I will always support you.
ejemplos.traduccion: Pase lo que pase, siempre te apoyaré.

ejemplos.frase: Suffice it to say that the evening did not end well.
ejemplos.traduccion: Baste decir que la velada no terminó bien.

ejemplos.frase: Far be it from me to tell you how to raise your children.
ejemplos.traduccion: Lejos de mí decirte cómo criar a tus hijos.

ejemplos.frase: We can sleep in the car if need be.
ejemplos.traduccion: Si hace falta, podemos dormir en el coche.

ejemplos.frase: He is, as it were, a prisoner of his own success.
ejemplos.traduccion: Es, por así decirlo, prisionero de su propio éxito.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Be as it may, we must continue.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Be that as it may, we must continue.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The fixed phrase is be that as it may; that cannot be left out.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Suffice to say it that he lost.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Suffice it to say that he lost.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The order is fixed: suffice it to say (suffice to say is also heard).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Whatever comes may, I'll be there.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Come what may, I'll be there.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: It is a fixed inversion with the base form: come what may.

ejercicios.frase: ___ that as it may, we still need a decision by Friday.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the point in Rules and key points that these phrases are frozen expressions: neither the person nor the tense changes. The clue is the structure “___ that as it may” followed by a comma, which is exactly the phrase be that as it may (“however that may be, even so”). The correct answer is be, the old subjunctive: the base form of the verb, placed before the subject that. It is used to acknowledge what has just been said and still carry on with the argument.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed phrase with the subjunctive: be that as it may.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sea como sea, seguimos necesitando una decisión antes del viernes.

por_opcion.Be: Correct: the fixed phrase is be that as it may, with the verb in the base form (subjunctive) before the subject.
por_opcion.Is: Incorrect: is is indicative and the phrase does not allow the verb to change; “Is that as it may” does not exist in English.
por_opcion.Being: Incorrect: the gerund does not form this expression; the phrase keeps the subjunctive be.
por_opcion.Was: Incorrect: the expression is frozen and is not put into the past even when the narrative is in the past.

ejercicios.frase: If that is the voters' choice, then so ___ it.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of frozen expressions from Rules and key points: so be it (“let it be so”) keeps the subjunctive be. The clue is the word so before the gap and the context of accepting someone else’s decision with resignation. The correct form is be, in the base form, because it is a wish or an acceptance, not a statement of fact. It is used above all to close a discussion by accepting something we do not like.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: So be it = let it be so, with the subjunctive be.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si esa es la elección de los votantes, entonces que así sea.

por_opcion.is: Incorrect: “so is it” would be a different (and odd) sentence; the phrase of acceptance takes the subjunctive be.
por_opcion.be: Correct: so be it is the fixed phrase, with be in the base form, expressing resigned acceptance.
por_opcion.was: Incorrect: the phrase is not put into the past; besides, “so was it” does not have this meaning.
por_opcion.will: Incorrect: will needs a verb after it and does not form this expression; “so will it” means something else (“it will too”).

ejercicios.frase: Far ___ it from me to question your judgement.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the phrase far be it from me to + infinitive from the table, one of the frozen expressions with the subjunctive. The clue is the beginning “Far ___ it from me to”, which only allows be in the base form before it. As noted in Rules and key points, this phrase usually introduces precisely what the speaker claims not to want to do: in practice, the person who uses it is questioning the other person’s judgement, but with ironic politeness.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Far be it from me to: I have no wish to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Lejos de mí la intención de poner en duda tu criterio.

por_opcion.is: Incorrect: “Far is it from me” breaks the phrase, which only allows the subjunctive be.
por_opcion.be: Correct: far be it from me to is the fixed phrase, with be in the base form before it.
por_opcion.was: Incorrect: the expression is not conjugated in the past; it is frozen in the subjunctive.
por_opcion.being: Incorrect: the gerund does not form the expression; “Far being it” does not exist.

ejercicios.frase: The team will be ready, come what ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of frozen expressions: the phrase is come what may (“whatever happens”), and Rules and key points expressly warns that the tense does not change. The clue is the expression “come what ___” at the end of the sentence, after a comma, which expresses determination in the face of any obstacle. The only possible form is may; any other modal produces a sentence that a native speaker perceives as wrong.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The phrase is come what may.
ejercicios.traduccion: El equipo estará listo, pase lo que pase.

por_opcion.may: Correct: come what may is the fixed phrase and allows no other modal.
por_opcion.might: Incorrect: although might may seem more “hypothetical”, the expression is frozen with may.
por_opcion.can: Incorrect: “come what can” does not exist; the modal in the phrase is may.
por_opcion.will: Incorrect: “come what will” is not the standard phrase; you say come what may.

ejercicios.frase: ___ it to say that the negotiations failed.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the phrase suffice it to say (that) from the table, with the verb suffice in the subjunctive before it. The clue is “___ it to say that”, which reproduces exactly the structure of the expression. The answer is Suffice, in the base form without -s, because it is a subjunctive expressing a wish (“let it be enough”). It is used to sum something up without giving details, often because they are unpleasant or obvious.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Suffice it to say: it is enough to say.
ejercicios.traduccion: Baste decir que las negociaciones fracasaron.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It adds the third-person indicative -s; the phrase uses the subjunctive, which is the base form suffice.
It is a literal copy of the Spanish “basta decir”; in English the fixed phrase requires the verb suffice.
It is an adjective, not the verb; the expression is Suffice it to say.

ejercicios.frase: We'll hire extra staff if need ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the expression if need be (“if it is necessary”) from the table, another frozen phrase with the subjunctive. The clue is “if need ___” at the end of the sentence. The correct form is be, in the base form even though need is a singular noun: you do not say “if need is”. It is a very useful, somewhat formal expression for saying that something will be done only if necessary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If need be: if it is necessary.
ejercicios.traduccion: Contrataremos personal extra si fuera necesario.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It uses the indicative; the phrase if need be is frozen with the subjunctive be.
It copies the Spanish “si se necesita”; in the phrase, need is the subject and the verb is be.
Although it looks like a subjunctive, the fixed expression is if need be, not “if need were”.

ejercicios.frase: She became, as it ___, the face of the campaign.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the expression as it were (“so to speak”) from the table, which keeps the subjunctive were. The clue is “as it ___” between commas, in the middle of the sentence, as an aside that softens a metaphor (the face of the campaign). The correct form is were even though the subject is it, because it is the old subjunctive and not the past indicative. It is a fixed phrase: you do not say “as it was” with this meaning.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: As it were: so to speak.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ella se convirtió, por así decirlo, en la cara de la campaña.

errores_previstos.explicacion: As it was exists, but it means “as things stood”; the aside meaning “so to speak” is as it were.
It uses the present indicative; the fixed phrase takes the subjunctive were.
It is another subjunctive form, but the specific expression is as it were.

ejercicios.frase: Heaven ___ that we should ever need to use these shelters.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the phrase heaven forbid / God forbid from the table (“I hope this never happens”). The clue is “Heaven ___ that…”, a negative wish about something we fear. The verb is in the base form, forbid, without -s, even though heaven is singular: it is the subjunctive of wishing, as in God save the Queen. It can be followed by a clause with that and should, as in the example on the card.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Heaven forbid: I hope this never happens.
ejercicios.traduccion: Dios no quiera que alguna vez tengamos que usar estos refugios.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It adds the indicative -s; in the phrase the verb is in the subjunctive, the base form forbid.
It uses the past participle; the expression requires the verb in the base form.
It is a synonym that does not form the fixed phrase; you say Heaven forbid.

glosario.definicion_l: a structure that provides privacy and protection from danger · protective covering that provides protection from the weather

ejercicios.frase: The decision now rests with the powers that ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the general rule of the card: remnants of the subjunctive in fixed expressions. The powers that be (“the people in authority”) keeps be in the base form instead of are. The clue is “the powers that ___”, a relative clause which, in this frozen expression, does not take a conjugated verb. It often has an ironic or resigned tone towards the anonymous authority that makes the decisions.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The powers that be: the people in authority.
ejercicios.traduccion: La decisión está ahora en manos de los que mandan.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It is the normal indicative form, but the fixed expression keeps the subjunctive: the powers that be.
As well as breaking the phrase, it does not agree with powers, which is plural.
It copies the Spanish “los que mandan”; the idiomatic expression is the powers that be.

glosario.significado: depender de, estar en manos de

ejercicios.frase: All employees, be ___ managers or interns, must attend the training.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the phrase be it… or… (“whether it is… or…”) from the table, which keeps the subjunctive be before the subject. The clue is the structure “be ___ managers or interns”, which presents two alternatives, and the antecedent all employees, which is plural and refers to people. That is why the inverted subject is they: be they managers or interns. With a singular antecedent or a thing, you use be it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Be they… or… = whether they are… or…; with a plural you use they.
ejercicios.traduccion: Todos los empleados, ya sean directivos o becarios, deben asistir a la formación.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Be it is used with a singular subject or a thing; here it refers to all employees, which is plural, so you need they.
After inverted be comes a subject pronoun, not an object pronoun: be they.
It copies the Spanish “ya sea”; the phrase needs the subject after be.

glosario.definicion_l: an advanced student or graduate in medicine gaining supervised practical experience · deprive of freedom

ejercicios.frase: Be this as it may, the plan goes ahead.
respuestas: Be that as it may, the plan goes ahead.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the point in Rules and key points: these are frozen expressions and no part of them changes. The fixed phrase is be that as it may, with that and not this, even though the Spanish “esto” might seem just as natural. The corrected sentence keeps the subjunctive be before that and the comma before the main clause. The mistake on the card (this) is a typical case of trying to adapt the phrase to the context.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The fixed phrase uses that, not this.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sea como sea, el plan sigue adelante.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Be this as it may, the plan goes ahead.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: the fixed phrase uses that, not this.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Be as it may, the plan goes ahead.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves out that, a mistake listed on the card; the full phrase is be that as it may.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Be that as it might, the plan goes ahead.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It changes may to might; the expression is frozen and allows no other modal.

ejercicios.frase: Come what might, I'm not giving up.
respuestas: Come what may, I'm not giving up.
Come what may, I am not giving up.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of frozen expressions: Rules and key points gives changing the tense as an example of a mistake, and here may has been changed to might. The correct expression is come what may, with come in the subjunctive at the front and the modal may. Both I'm not giving up and I am not giving up are accepted, because the contraction does not affect the phrase. It expresses determination: nothing is going to prevent what is being said.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The fixed expression is come what may.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pase lo que pase, no me voy a rendir.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Come what might, I'm not giving up.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It leaves the sentence uncorrected: the fixed phrase is come what may.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Whatever comes may, I'm not giving up.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the mistake listed on the card: it mixes whatever with the phrase, which is come what may.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Come what will, I'm not giving up.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It changes the modal; the fixed expression only allows may.

respuestas: Far be it from me to complain
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the phrase far be it from me to + infinitive from the table, whose order is fixed: far, the subjunctive be, the subject it, from me and to + verb. The clue is that you are given the exact parts of the expression and an infinitive, complain. As Rules and key points notes, the phrase usually introduces what the speaker claims not to want to do, so it is often followed by a “but…”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed order: far be it from me to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Lejos de mí la intención de quejarme.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Far from me be it to complain
errores_previstos.explicacion: It copies the order of the Spanish “lejos de mí”; the fixed phrase puts be it right after far.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It be far from me to complain
errores_previstos.explicacion: It uses the normal subject-verb order; the phrase inverts it: Far be it.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of frozen expressions: be that as it may has a fixed order, with the subjunctive be before that and as it may after it. The clue is that the five words are exactly those of the phrase in the table. It cannot be reordered like a normal sentence and no part can be changed; it is used at the beginning of the sentence to acknowledge an argument and carry on in spite of it.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It puts the subject first as in a normal sentence; the phrase inverts the order: Be that.
It mixes up the parts; the fixed order is Be that as it may.

descripcion_larga_es: Some English expressions keep the old subjunctive: the verb appears in the base form (be, come, suffice) and often before the subject. They cannot be created freely; they are learnt as closed blocks. They give a formal, solemn or ironic tone that is very useful for qualifying or concluding an idea in a presentation, but any change (this for that, might for may) immediately gives away a non-native speaker.

contexto.que_es: They are fixed phrases that keep the Old English subjunctive: the verb is in the base form without -s or past tense (be, come, suffice, forbid) and often with verb + subject order. They work as frozen pieces, just like the Spanish “sea como sea”, “así sea” or “Dios no lo quiera”.
contexto.por_que_importa: They appear in speeches, the quality press, essays and formal spoken English, and they allow you to qualify, concede or conclude an argument elegantly. Because they are fixed blocks, any variation (be this as it may, come what might) immediately sounds wrong. In a high-level oral exam, used well, they add richness of register, but overusing them sounds pedantic.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They are used to concede and move on to another idea (be that as it may), show determination (come what may), accept something with resignation (so be it), sum up without going into detail (suffice it to say) or introduce a criticism with false modesty (far be it from me to). Spanish speakers tend to “regularise” them by putting the verb in the indicative (is, was) or in another tense, which is exactly what these phrases do not allow.
